exercises.title: Differentiate a Logistic Loss
exercises.focus: A derivative as sensitivity; stable scalar loss; central differences
exercises.why: Gradient descent needs the direction in which changing a parameter changes the loss. A numerical derivative gives you an independent check before trusting a training loop.
exercises.brief: Start with one prediction: score z = w*x + b. Convert the score into probability p = sigmoid(z) of label y=1. The binary logistic loss is softplus(z) - y*z, where softplus(z)=log(1+exp(z)). Implement loss_and_grad(w,b,x,y), returning (loss, dloss/dw, dloss/db), and central_difference(f,theta,eps=1e-5), returning [f(theta+eps)-f(theta-eps)]/(2*eps). y must be 0 or 1; eps must be positive, otherwise raise ValueError. All other inputs are finite scalars. Calculate the w=b=0 case by hand first. Keep loss and gradients finite at scores +/-1000; directly exponentiating a large positive score will overflow. Check your analytic gradients against central differences over varied inputs. This is the primitive used later to verify policy and preference objectives.

exercises.title: Train and Diagnose a Tiny Regressor
exercises.focus: Online SGD; simultaneous parameter updates; measurable learning
exercises.why: A loss function is only useful when the optimizer really learns. This drill makes learning measurable before introducing tensors, accelerators, or larger models.
exercises.brief: Fit y_hat=w*x+b to pairs (x,y). Implement mse(data,w,b), the mean of squared errors, and train(data,lr,epochs), returning {'w':float,'b':float,'losses':list}. Start w=b=0. For each epoch, visit examples in the given order and take ONE stochastic gradient step per example on (w*x+b-y)^2, without the 1/2 convention. Compute both parameter gradients using the same pre-update error. losses includes full-dataset MSE at initialization and after each epoch, length epochs+1. Do not shuffle. Reject empty data, negative lr, and epochs that are negative or not integers with ValueError; lr=0 and epochs=0 are valid. Inputs are finite. Predict what a zero learning rate does, then show learning on y=2*x+1 and a second unseen slope. A loss may rise with an excessive learning rate; do not hardcode a decreasing curve.

exercises.title: Turn Scores into a Policy Gradient
exercises.focus: Stable categorical probabilities; log probability; REINFORCE
exercises.why: Policies assign probabilities to actions. You will learn how one observed advantage changes those probabilities and verify that direction numerically.
exercises.brief: A policy chooses one action from a finite list. Its logits are arbitrary real scores; softmax converts them to positive probabilities summing to 1. Implement softmax(logits), log_prob(logits,action), and reinforce_loss_grad(logits,action,advantage), returning (loss, gradient_list). The objective to MINIMIZE for one sample is -advantage*log_prob(action). Advantage is how much better that action performed than its baseline; treat it as a constant. logits must be a nonempty list of finite scalars; action must be an integer index in range, otherwise ValueError. Compute log probability directly using log-sum-exp so an action with score -1000 can have a finite log probability even if its probability underflows. A common shift of every score must not change the policy. Explain why a positive advantage should increase the selected action's probability after gradient descent. Background: https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/spinningup/rl_intro3.html

exercises.title: Compute Advantages Across Episode Boundaries
exercises.focus: Temporal difference residuals; bootstrapping; terminated versus truncated
exercises.why: A silent episode-boundary error can change what an RL algorithm learns. This drill forces you to reason about value estimates and trajectory bookkeeping separately.
exercises.brief: Implement gae(rewards,values,next_values,terminated,truncated,gamma,lam), returning (advantages,returns), both lists. All five sequences must have equal lengths; empty aligned sequences return ([],[]). gamma and lam lie in [0,1]; invalid lengths or coefficients raise ValueError. values[t] estimates remaining discounted reward BEFORE action t. next_values[t] is the estimate at the actual successor observation, including a time-limit final observation before reset. terminated[t] means the task truly ended: do NOT bootstrap it. truncated[t] means a rollout ended because of a time limit: DO bootstrap it, but do NOT carry the next episode's advantage backward across that boundary. Define delta[t]=reward[t]+gamma*(0 if terminated[t] else next_values[t])-values[t]. In reverse order, A[t]=delta[t]+gamma*lam*A[t+1] only if neither boundary flag is true; use A beyond the supplied batch=0. returns[t]=A[t]+values[t]. If both flags are true, termination wins. Calculate a two-transition example before coding. Source: https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html

exercises.title: Implement the Sign-Aware PPO Objective
exercises.focus: Importance ratio; pessimistic clipping; loss sign and diagnostics
exercises.why: An objective can look plausible while rewarding the wrong policy update. This drill checks the asymmetric effect of clipping for positive and negative advantages.
exercises.brief: Implement ppo_loss(old_logp,new_logp,advantages,clip_eps=.2), returning {'loss':float,'clip_fraction':float,'approx_kl':float}. The lists are aligned, nonempty finite scalars; clip_eps is in [0,1), otherwise ValueError. For each sample ratio r=exp(new-old), clipped_r=clamp(r,1-eps,1+eps), and surrogate=min(r*A,clipped_r*A). Return the NEGATIVE MEAN surrogate for gradient descent. Do not simply clip r in every case: when A is negative, a different side of the update becomes capped. clip_fraction counts ratios strictly outside the interval, regardless of the sign of A. approx_kl is mean((r-1)-(new-old)), a sample diagnostic, not an exact distribution KL. Log-ratio differences are limited to [-50,50] for this exercise. Describe in DESIGN.md why r=.5,A=-1 is capped but r=2,A=-1 remains penalized, using the two candidate surrogates explicitly. Original PPO paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347

exercises.title: Build and Check a DPO Preference Loss
exercises.focus: Reference-relative preference margin; stable logistic objective; beta sensitivity
exercises.why: Post-training work needs precise objectives and sensitivity checks. Here you optimize a preferred-vs-rejected response pair without building a separate reward model.
exercises.brief: Each input is the SUM of token log probabilities for a complete response, already computed upstream. Implement dpo_loss(policy_chosen,policy_rejected,reference_chosen,reference_rejected,beta=.1), returning (loss,margin,grad_chosen,grad_rejected). margin=beta*((policy_chosen-policy_rejected)-(reference_chosen-reference_rejected)). loss=-log(sigmoid(margin)); gradients are with respect to the two policy log probabilities, holding the reference fixed. beta must be finite and positive or raise ValueError; all four log probabilities are finite. Use a stable logistic expression for margins +/-1000. An improved policy chosen/rejected log-ratio should reduce loss relative to the same reference. Adding a shared offset to both policy log probabilities should not change the result. Explain why this tiny primitive omits token masking, sequence length conventions, data quality, and training evaluation; these are requirements of the later full project. Original DPO paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290

exercises.title: Measure a Quantized Linear Layer
exercises.focus: Per-row int8 quantization; reconstruction bounds; output error
exercises.why: ML infrastructure research compares measured accuracy with memory and runtime costs. You will establish the numerical side of that tradeoff on a layer small enough to inspect.
exercises.brief: Implement quantize_rows(weights) -> (qrows,scales), dequantize_rows(qrows,scales) -> float rows, and quantized_matvec(qrows,scales,x) -> output vector. weights is a nonempty rectangular matrix with nonempty rows of finite floats. Per row, scale=max(abs(w))/127, with scale=1 for an all-zero row. Use Python round (ties to even), then clamp to [-127,127] to form integer q. Reconstruct w_hat=q*scale; perform the matrix-vector product using this reconstruction. Validate nonempty rectangular shapes, one finite positive scale per row, integer q in [-127,127], and matching x width; raise ValueError on violation. Empty or ragged matrices are invalid. Compute a full-precision baseline in your own test. For each output row, verify absolute error <= scale/2 * sum(abs(x)) plus floating-point tolerance. Report both absolute and relative error; relative error near a zero baseline can be misleading. This pure-Python drill does not claim speedups: real kernel benchmarking belongs in the later systems project.

exercises.title: Evaluate a Point-Reach Controller
exercises.focus: Discrete dynamics; bounded actions; held-out rollout metrics
exercises.why: Robot learning requires accurate environment semantics and honest evaluation before adding a learned policy. This drill builds a deterministic baseline and records its trajectories.
exercises.brief: This is a simulated point moving in 2D, not physical robot control. Implement step(position,action,dt=0.1,max_speed=1.0): clip EACH action component independently into [-max_speed,max_speed], then return a new [x+dt*ux,y+dt*uy] without mutating inputs. Implement rollout(start,target,gain,steps,dt=.1,max_speed=1.): before each step choose action=gain*(target-position); return positions including start, length steps+1. Implement evaluate(targets,gain,steps,dt=.1,max_speed=1.,tolerance=.05): run every target from [0,0], return {'success_rate':fraction with final distance <= tolerance,'mean_final_distance':float,'mean_path_length':float}. Path length sums Euclidean segment lengths; do not substitute start-to-end displacement. targets is a nonempty list of 2D targets. All coordinates are finite. Reject non-2D vectors, nonpositive dt or max_speed, negative gain or tolerance, and steps that are negative or not integers with ValueError. steps=0 is valid. Use math.hypot for distances. Tune gain on your own training target list, then freeze it and evaluate a disjoint held-out list; never report tuning targets as held-out. This controller is a baseline for a later learned-policy project, not evidence of robot-learning mastery.
